artifacts.caption: Minkowski spacetime diagram — Einstein's 1905 relativity in one drawing.
artifacts.credit: Stib at English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0
artifacts.description: Minkowski diagram explaining the world line of a photon: a 45° line on a space-time graph where the time axis is ct and the space axis is x. The diagonals are the light cone; events inside it are timelike, outside are spacelike. This is the diagram Einstein was looking at when he wrote the special relativity paper.

artifacts.caption: World lines — a stationary clock's vertical line; a moving clock's tilted line.
artifacts.credit: Self-made, transferred from en.wikipedia. CC BY-SA 3.0
artifacts.description: Spacetime diagram showing two world lines: a stationary observer (vertical) and an observer moving at velocity v (tilted). The hyperbola between them is the locus of events that are one unit of proper time from the origin. Minkowski's 1908 paper used this exact construction to show that elapsed time is frame-dependent.

artifacts.caption: USNO Master Clock — the cesium fountain that keeps the official US time.
artifacts.description: The USNO Master Clock is an ensemble of more than 100 cesium-beam and hydrogen-maser atomic clocks at the US Naval Observatory in Washington, DC. The ensemble defines UTC(USNO), the official time reference for the US Department of Defense. Each cesium clock measures the 9,192,631,770 Hz transition that defines the SI second.

artifacts.caption: The 'Henlein-Uhr' — c. 1510, Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg.
artifacts.description: One of the first pocket watches, attributed (controversially) to Peter Henlein of Nuremberg, c. 1510. Iron and brass, fire-gilded, 5.2 cm diameter, 174 g. The signature 'Petrus Hele me f(ecit) Norimb(erga) 1510' is widely considered a later addition, but the watch itself is the oldest portable spring-driven timepiece in any museum.

artifacts.caption: Seiko Quartz-Astron 35SQ — the first quartz wristwatch, 25 December 1969.
artifacts.description: The Seiko Quartz-Astron 35SQ, the first commercial quartz wristwatch, sold in Tokyo on 25 December 1969. 100 pieces. 8192 Hz quartz oscillator, hybrid integrated circuit, phase-locked stepping motor. An IEEE Milestone. Deutsches Uhrenmuseum inventory number 2012-047.

artifacts.caption: Seiko Cal. 35A — the movement inside the Astron, world's first quartz caliber.
artifacts.description: Seiko Caliber 35A, the world's first production quartz movement. Used in the Seiko Astron (1969). 8192 Hz XY-cut quartz oscillator, hybrid IC, phase-locked stepping motor. The battery is the silver cylinder on the right; the quartz can is the small disc visible in the lower center.

artifacts.file: Watch in the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum (15845457165).jpg
artifacts.caption: 8:15 — the watch that stopped at the moment of the first atomic bombing, 6 August 1945.
artifacts.description: A wristwatch on display at the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum. The hands stopped at 8:15 a.m. — the exact time the first nuclear weapon was used in warfare, 6 August 1945. Donated by Akito Kawagoe, who was 1,700 m from the hypocenter. The watch is the museum's most-cited single artifact; it is also the saddest watch in any collection.
